EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm impacted much of southeast South Carolina with significant snow accumulations and very cold wind chill temperatures. An area of low pressure shifted off the Southeast coast while deepening, ushering in a very cold air mass across the region. The depth of cold air was sufficient to support snow as the primary precipitation type. Rain quickly transitioned to snow during the afternoon hours, which continued into the evening before ending. Most of the snow accumulation impacted areas along and north of Interstate 16, with the highest amounts reported across Screven, Bulloch, and Effingham counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread snow produced accumulations of 2 to 4 inches across the inland portion of Jasper County. The highest reported amounts include 4 inches in the Pineland area and 2.5 inches in Ridgeland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A unique snow setup for South Carolina developed as a strong coastal low strengthening offshore, while a upper level disturbance shifted over our area. This provided sufficient synoptic and mesoscale lift for widespread heavy snow across SC along with unusually high snow to liquid ratios between 15-20 to 1. A brief period of sleet-graupel occurred at the onset of the event following by 12 hours of light-moderate snow across the area, with highest amounts in the Pee Dee region of SC.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple CoCoRAHS observers across Edgefield county measured between 2.5 and 3 inches of snowfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With strong cold air damming in place, areas of light drizzle developed in the presence of surface temperatures at or just below freezing in portions of southeast South Carolina. The cold air was quite shallow, providing an ideal temperature profile for freezing rain and freezing drizzle. The event occurred in the early morning hours before surface temperatures warmed above freezing and the drizzle came to an end. Only light ice amounts were observed, with only limited impacts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light freezing rain and freezing drizzle produced a light glaze of ice, mostly on elevated and exposed surfaces across the county. The light glaze of ice did produce a slippery stretch of roadway on Interstate 26 between mile marker 181 and 182 where an overturned vehicle was reported. There was one report of a few hundredths of an inch of ice accumulation on leaves in the Reevesville area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation associated with an intensifying low pressure system over the Deep South developed in areas along and near the Blue Ridge escarpment during the late evening of the 24th, beginning mainly as sleet. The sleet, occasionally mixed with snow continued into the early morning of the 25th, when it began to mix with and eventually change to freezing rain. The freezing rain was mostly light until a band of heavy freezing rain moved over the area late in the afternoon. Total sleet accumulations of 1 to 2 inches occurred, with around 0.5 inch (locally as high as 0.75 inch) ice accretion on top of the sleet, resulting in very hazardous driving conditions. Unusually cold temperatures following the event resulted in travel difficulties that lingered for several days.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A classic ice storm setup developed across the Midlands of South Carolina January 25th. Cold air damming at the surface and strong overrunning aloft produced light and moderate freezing across the Central Midlands with sleet predominant in the Northern Midlands. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree and powerline damage near Cheraw resulting in roughly 1000 power outages due to storm damage.

The environment ahead of this system was characterized by sufficient instability with MLCAPE values around 500 J/kg, 0-1km SRH values of 100-200 m2s2 and 0-6km shear of 60 knots. This environment combined with strong forcing supported a QLCS line that moved across the forecast area during the morning hours. Several damaging wind reports and a few tornadoes occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The NWS has confirmed an EF-0 tornado in Ridge Spring, SC based on a public report and corresponding strong velocity couplet from KCAE radar. The tornado formed east of Ridge Spring Hwy and south of Murphy Farm Rd. While a survey was not conducted, pictures of the damage show multiple hardwood trees uprooted and partial loss of metal roofing on a small barn.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm impacted much of southeast South Carolina with significant snow accumulations on January 31st along with very cold wind chill temperatures persisting into late morning February 1st. An area of low pressure shifted off the Southeast Coast while deepening, ushering in a very cold air mass across the region. The depth of cold air was sufficient to support snow as the primary precipitation type during afternoon and evening hours on January 31st. Snow accumulation ended by midnight on January 31st, but hazardous traveling conditions and very cold wind chill temperatures persisted through morning hours on February 1st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The local criteria for an Extreme Cold Warning is temperature or wind chill of 10 degrees or less. A wind chill temperature of 10 degrees or less was ongoing at the Beaufort Marine Corps Air Station (KNBC), the Beaufort WeatherSTEM site (1190W) and the Beaufort Weatherflow site (XBUF) at 12 AM EST. The wind chill temperature first fell to 10 degrees or less at the Calibogue Sound Weatherflow site (XCLB) at 236 AM EST and at the Hilton Head Island Airport (KHXB) at 455 AM EST. The South Carolina Department of Public Health reported a fatality due to hypothermia associated with this event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation associated with an intensifying low pressure system over the Deep South developed across the South Carolina Piedmont during the early morning of the 25th. The precipitation began as mostly sleet before mixing with, and eventually changing to freezing rain later in the morning. The precipitation finally tapered off during the evening. Total sleet accumulations of 0.25 to 0.5 inches occurred, with around 0.25 inch of ice accreting on top of the sleet. This made for very hazardous driving conditions. Due to unusually cold weather following the event, a couple of days of refreezing resulted in travel difficulties continuing during the overnight and morning hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With strong cold air damming in place, areas of light drizzle developed in the presence of surface temperatures at or just below freezing in portions of southeast South Carolina. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of strong thunderstorms developed just ahead of a strong cold front and moved into southeast South Carolina in the morning hours. The environment ahead of these storms was supportive of damaging wind gusts and an isolated tornado. A few of the clusters of thunderstorms became strong enough to produce severe weather, including a weak tornado in Allendale County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS Storm Survey team confirmed that an EF-0 tornado occurred in northern Allendale County near Millett with estimated peak wind speeds of 80 mph. The initial damage occurred near Speedwell Methodist Church near the intersection of Millett Road and Little Hell Road. Damage at the beginning of the tornado path consisted of a few uprooted trees. The tornado then tracked to the northeast across a very large field, crossing Furse Mill Road. A well build out building along Furse Mill Road had its roof removed, with several nearby large pine trees either snapped or uprooted. The tornado then damaged a family farm off of Highway 125, peeling tin roof material off of 4 to 5 pole barns and garages. Additional tree damage was noted in the area, though some of the damage was likely old and associated with Hurricane Helene. The tornado then reached a home site near the intersection of Patterson Mill Drive and Ellis Road. Two very large trees were uprooted in the front yard of the house, with some additional tree damage in the backyard. The track of the tornado damage ended along Ellis Road in a forested area. A clear convergent pattern was noted with numerous snapped or uprooted hardwood trees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A protracted period of abnormally dry weather that began in autumn of 2025 and continued through the winter culminated in extreme drought conditions across much of  upstate South Carolina by early spring. Monthly precipitation was anywhere from 25 percent to 75 percent of normal for seven consecutive months beginning in September 2025. The September through March period was one of the top 5 driest on record across much of the area. Portions of the Piedmont saw their driest September-through-March on record. Unusually warm weather in March and April of 2026 further contributed to evolving drought conditions. Both months were among the top 5 warmest on record at most major climate sites across the region. By early April, streamflow across the region was 25 to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture levels were extremely low and only poor-to-fair crop conditions were reported during the critical spring planting period. Despite the very warm and dry conditions, occurrence of large wildfires was limited, likely due to a statewide burn ban that was instituted in late March.

A similar environment to 5/24 took shape during the afternoon of 5/25, continuing into the late evening. Seasonal instability brought summertime pulse convection that was slow moving with efficient rain rates as PWAT's neared 2. This led to a couple instances of flash flooding in southern Lancaster County, SC early in the afternoon before bringing a couple more instances later in the evening near Augusta GA.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A southern stream shortwave phased with a digging northern stream upper trough over the OH/TN valleys the night of 3/11 into the morning of 3/12 bringing a strongly forced system into the forecast area. The environment ahead of this system was characterized by sufficient instability with MLCAPE values around 500 J/kg, 0-1km SRH values of 100-200 m2s2 and 0-6km shear of 60 knots. This environment combined with strong forcing supported a QLCS line that moved across the forecast area during the morning hours. Several damaging wind reports and a few tornadoes occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A NWS Survey Team confirmed a brief EF-0 tornado south of the town of Bamberg in Bamberg County, SC from March 12th, 2026. The tornado formed near the intersection of HWY 601 and Harley Rd and continued east along Harley Road. Most of the damage occurred on a property at the intersection of HWY 601 and Harley Rd where multiple trees were downed and one large pine tree trunk was found snapped. The tornado continued into a field to the east, evident in the grass leaning in opposite directions, and lifted before reaching a wooded area east of the field.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of storms developed during the afternoon of 6/14 along strong low level convergence associated with a prefrontal trough. Moderate instability with MLCAPE around 1500 J/kg and enhancement from an outflow boundary led to damaging wind gusts in a portion of the line.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SC Highway Patrol reported a tree down at Salley Rd and Ellison Estates Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur moved into the southeastern US which led to a significant surge of moisture into the area. The air mass became highly unstable in the afternoon and evening with MLCAPE values around 2500 J/kg. While there were isolated severe storms during the afternoon, widespread storms developed along a surface trough in Georgia with strong low level convergence which led to a line that moved through the area producing damaging wind gusts during the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SC Emergency Management Division employee reported the top third of a mature pine tree downed near the corner of Meadowood Rd and Sylvan Dr.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong destabilization occurred over the area with MLCAPE rising to above 2500 J/kg and deep layer shear around 20 knots. Scattered thunderstorms developed along a weak surface trough through the afternoon into the evening. Most of these storms produced sub-severe wind gusts but one storm reached severe limits.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SC Highway Patrol reported a tree down on Glenwood Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak upper shortwave moved through the area during the afternoon of 6/27. With a moderate to strong destabilization with MLCAPE approaching 2000 J/kg, scattered thunderstorms developed across the area. A favorable downburst environment was in place with strong low level lapse rates and DCAPE between 700-800 J/kg. While most downbursts were sub-severe, one storm reached severe limits.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Aiken County Dispatch reported trees fell on a power line leading to a fire near the  intersection of Kathwood Rd and Old Jackson Hwy.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave embedded in a weakness in an upper ridge led to a MCS developing in the Tennessee Valley that moved into the forecast area late afternoon. While this system was decaying as it reached the area, it produced severe wind gusts in Lancaster, SC.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lancaster County Sheriff reported a tree down on Kings Circle.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the early morning hours on April 30th a line of thunderstorms moved through the Central Savannah River Area producing an isolated incident of wind damage in the vicinity of the Savannah River Site where a 200ft tower measured a wind gust of 78 mph. The atmosphere was weakly unstable with SBCAPE values approaching 1000 J/kg and 0-6km shear around 40 knots. PWAT values were around 1.3 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Aiken County Sheriff Office reported trees down along Hwy 278 and Boggy Gut Rd. Time estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A protracted period of abnormally dry weather that began in autumn of 2025 and continued through the winter culminated in extreme drought conditions across much of  upstate South Carolina by early spring. Monthly precipitation was anywhere from 25 percent to 75 percent of normal for seven consecutive months beginning in September 2025. The September through March period was one of the top 5 driest on record across much of the area. Portions of the Piedmont saw their driest September-through-March on record. Unusually warm weather in March and April of 2026 further contributed to evolving drought conditions. Both months were among the top 5 warmest on record at most major climate sites across the region. By early April, streamflow across the region was 25 to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture levels were extremely low and only poor-to-fair crop conditions were reported during the critical spring planting period. Despite the very warm and dry conditions, occurrence of large wildfires was limited, likely due to a statewide burn ban that was instituted in late March.

A diffuse frontal boundary stalled across the northern forecast area 5/22 with broad troughing present. Areas south of the boundary saw generous heating with MLCAPE values nearing 1500-2000 J/kg and weak deep layer shear near 25-30 kts. This heating across the boundary lead to a couple strong storms, but one that produced tree damage near Thomson GA and started a fire at McCormick High School in McCormick County SC.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: McCormick County Emergency Services reported a structure fire at the McCormick County  High School gym due to a lightning strike.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A lingering stalled front remained in the forecast area 5/23, but a embedded shortwave in the general troughing pattern moved in during the afternoon and evening hours, leading to scattered convection to develop. The environment ahead of this shortwave was characterized by MLCAPE values over 2000 J/kg and effective shear near 30-35 kts. Scattered strong to severe storms moved across the forecast area during the afternoon and evening hours, bringing damaging winds, hail up to golf ball sized, and even a report of a waterspout over Lake Murray in SC.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A broken line of thunderstorms formed along an outflow boundary and moved across the northern half of Lake Marion the evening of 5/23. Estimated winds from these thunderstorms were up to 35 kts. As these storms pushed across the lake, a women was fatally wounded from being struck by an umbrella at the Driftwood Grill restaurant on the eastern shore of Lake Marion. Report received from local media, time estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a near-record dry April, the impacts of months-long precipitation deficits as high as 18 resulted in extreme to exceptional drought conditions lingering into May across the Upstate and Piedmont of South Carolina. Many pastures and hayfields were rated poor-to-very poor, resulting in forage shortages. Crop stress affected soybeans, delayed or reduced planting for corn and other crops, and lowered vegetable yields. Reservoirs, lakes, and streams were well below normal. Mandatory or voluntary conservation measures were in place in multiple systems, and some ponds and smaller supplies were critically low. Fire danger remained abnormally high and the wildfire season extended into May across the mountains, although the threat steadily decreased during the first half of the month owing to greenup and a continued statewide burn ban. A transition to a very wet pattern finally brought some relief late in the month, as May rainfall wound up 150 to 200% of normal. Some locations across the lower Piedmont received around 300% of normal May rainfall. Drought category was reduced to moderate-to-severe across the area by the start of June.

Many pastures and hayfields were rated poor-to-very poor, resulting in forage shortages. Crop stress affected soybeans, delayed or reduced planting for corn and other crops, and lowered vegetable yields. Reservoirs, lakes, and streams were well below normal. Mandatory or voluntary conservation measures were in place in multiple systems, and some ponds and smaller supplies were critically low.
